concept.name: Cumulative return
concept.definition: The total return of an investment over a multi-period horizon, obtained by compounding (geometrically linking) the single-period returns, assuming gains are reinvested. It measures the full change in value from the start to the end of the holding period.
concept.intuition: It is the answer to 'if I invested $1 at the start and reinvested everything, what fraction do I have now, minus one?' It compounds, so it is not the sum of the periodic returns.
concept.mechanics: Multiply the gross returns (growth factors) of each sub-period together and subtract one. Equivalently, sum the log returns over the horizon and exponentiate minus one.
concept.formula: R_cum = PRODUCT_{t=1..T} (1 + R_t) - 1, where R_t are the per-period simple returns; equivalently R_cum = exp(SUM r_t) - 1 using log returns r_t.
concept.failure_modes: Cumulative returns are path-dependent with respect to cash flows: with deposits and withdrawals, the simple compounded figure misstates performance and time-weighted or money-weighted methods are needed. Long cumulative figures also conceal interim drawdowns.
concept.misconceptions: Cumulative return is not the sum or arithmetic average of periodic returns: four annual returns of +50%, -20%, +30%, -40% sum to +20% but compound to a cumulative return of 1.5*0.8*1.3*0.6 - 1 = -6.4%.
concept.example: Monthly returns of +2%, -1%, and +3% give a cumulative return of 1.02 * 0.99 * 1.03 - 1 = 4.03% over the quarter.
